esp32-bike-light.title: ESP32-S3 Bicycle Light | Derek Nolt
esp32-bike-light.description: Building an ESP32-S3 bicycle light and BLE remote: LED rendering, packet validation, sensor bring-up, and the path from bench hardware to an enclosure.
esp32-bike-light.body:
DN Derek Nolt
  • About
  • Experience
  • Projects
  • Skills
  • Contact
← All projects

Embedded Systems

ESP32-S3 Bicycle Light

Building an ESP32-S3 bicycle light and BLE remote: LED rendering, packet validation, sensor bring-up, and the path from bench hardware to an enclosure.

By Derek Nolt

A bicycle light as an embedded-systems project

This project pairs an ESP32-S3 bicycle light with a two-button handlebar remote. It brings together LED effects, wireless input, motion-sensor diagnostics, and custom hardware design. The current work is a bench prototype: remote-controlled lighting is implemented, while automatic brake detection and several production features remain unfinished.

The firmware uses C++17 with Arduino and PlatformIO, with shared protocol and utility code for the two devices. Separate build environments keep the digital strip, analog development LEDs, wireless experiments, and enclosure hardware from becoming one ambiguous configuration.

The bench hardware

The physical digital prototype uses a 22-pixel WS2812B strip driven from GPIO18 through a 220-ohm series resistor. The sensor connects over I²C on GPIO9 and GPIO10. The handlebar remote uses active-low buttons on GPIO5 and GPIO6 with external 10-kilohm pull-ups.

The recorded bench setup powers the strip from a separate regulated 5 V supply and shares ground with the USB-powered ESP32. Direct 3.3 V data to the strip is a temporary bench arrangement; a 74HCT125 level shifter is planned. That distinction matters when moving from a working experiment to an electrical design that needs predictable margins.

Render frames without blocking the control logic

The scheduler requests an LED frame every 17 ms and an IMU sample every 10 ms. Animation is calculated from state and time instead of a sequence of delays. The NeoPixel transfer is still synchronous, so this is not a claim that every operation runs asynchronously.

The renderer applies brightness scaling, gamma 2.0 correction, and a software current estimate. For the 22-pixel build, the default brightness is 24/255, the hard ceiling is 128/255, and the estimated LED budget is capped at 700 mA. The model assumes 1 mA idle per pixel and 20 mA per full-scale color channel. This is an estimate used to limit output, not a substitute for a measured current trace or a hardware protection circuit.

In the current digital wireless implementation, the light starts steady red. A left or right press latches an amber wave; pressing the same side cancels it and pressing the other side switches direction. Simultaneous presses toggle hazards. The wave moves outward from the center with a three-pixel fading tail and a 560 ms period.

A six-byte BLE message

The development BLE protocol carries the current button state and a sequence number. Its compact layout makes validation explicit:

Offset  Size  Meaning
0       2     ASCII signature: BL
2       1     Protocol version: 1
3       1     Button mask: two low bits
4       2     Sequence number: little-endian uint16

The receiver checks length, signature, version, and allowed button bits. It uses wrap-aware sequence comparison to reject duplicate or older packets. The remote publishes approximately every 100 ms from a FreeRTOS task. A 600 ms freshness lease prevents an old button state from being treated as a new input.

Buttons are debounced for 30 ms, and both must be released after startup or reconnection before new input takes effect. The current digital light intentionally keeps a latched turn active through release or disconnection. Input freshness and the displayed signal are separate state decisions. Development BLE is currently unbonded; authenticated production pairing, stored peer identity, and application-level acknowledgements remain future work.

The sensor identity check caught a real mismatch

One of the more useful debugging moments came from a breakout presented as an MPU6050. It responded at I²C address 0x68, but its WHO_AM_I register returned 0x74, rather than the expected 0x68. The firmware rejected that identity instead of silently treating a responding address as proof of the expected sensor.

Support for the MPU6515 variant was then added. The project records include 67 fresh finite samples from an early bench capture and 301 fresh samples from a later stationary calibration. Sensor communication and calibration are milestones, but they do not establish reliable braking detection on a moving bicycle.

Another bench failure produced I²C NACKs because the ESP32 had been removed from the perfboard. Reseating it restored the expected identity and samples alongside LED frames. That is a useful reminder to verify the physical test arrangement before changing a driver.

What has been checked, and what still needs the bike

The repository records 48 native tests passing for the later wireless changes, along with bench logs showing increasing accepted BLE packets, zero rejected packets in that capture, and valid IMU samples. These are recorded results from the project, not new hardware tests performed for this article.

Automatic braking, motion wake and sleep, measured battery runtime, and assembled-device radio range still need implementation or validation. A successful desk test does not answer how the light behaves under vibration, changing orientation, weather, or a weak wireless link.

Moving toward a custom enclosure

The next hardware revision has editable KiCad and FreeCAD designs for a compact enclosure with a bonded plexiglass face, gasket, rear-access screws, and a mounted PCB. It targets an ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N16R8, 32 low-current WS2812C-2020 LEDs, and an LSM6DSOX motion sensor through a separate light_enclosure firmware target.

That target uses its own LED current model and sensor configuration rather than inheriting the bench strip’s assumptions. The mechanical and PCB files describe a designed prototype, not a finished, environmentally validated product. Keeping those revisions explicit makes the next round of bring-up easier to reason about.

Home / Services / Penetration Testing
🔒

Penetration Testing

Ethical hacking services to identify vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them. Simulate real-world attacks to test your defenses.

What is Penetration Testing?

Penetration testing, also known as ethical hacking, is a simulated cyber attack against your systems to check for exploitable vulnerabilities. Our certified ethical hackers use the same tools and techniques as malicious attackers to identify security weaknesses before they can be exploited.

This proactive approach helps organizations understand their real-world security posture and provides concrete evidence of vulnerabilities that need immediate attention.

Testing Types

Network Penetration Testing

Comprehensive testing of network infrastructure, including firewalls, routers, switches, and network services.

Web Application Testing

In-depth security testing of web applications, APIs, and web services to identify OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities.

Mobile Application Testing

Security assessment of iOS and Android applications, including static and dynamic analysis.

Wireless Network Testing

Assessment of wireless network security, including WiFi, Bluetooth, and other wireless protocols.

Social Engineering Testing

Controlled testing of human factors through phishing simulations and social engineering attacks.

Physical Security Testing

Assessment of physical security controls, including access controls, surveillance, and facility security.

Our Testing Methodology

1

Pre-Engagement

Define scope, rules of engagement, and obtain proper authorization before testing begins.

2

Reconnaissance

Gather information about target systems using passive and active reconnaissance techniques.

3

Scanning & Enumeration

Identify live systems, open ports, services, and potential entry points into the target environment.

4

Exploitation

Attempt to exploit identified vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to systems and data.

5

Post-Exploitation

Assess the impact of successful exploits and attempt to escalate privileges or move laterally.

6

Reporting

Document all findings with proof-of-concept exploits and provide remediation recommendations.

Testing Approaches

Black Box Testing: No prior knowledge of the target system, simulating an external attacker's perspective.

White Box Testing: Full knowledge of system architecture and source code, providing comprehensive internal assessment.

Gray Box Testing: Limited knowledge of the system, simulating an insider threat or compromised user scenario.

Deliverables

Executive Summary: High-level overview of findings and business risk assessment for leadership.

Technical Report: Detailed documentation of all vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept exploits.

Remediation Guide: Step-by-step instructions for fixing identified vulnerabilities.

Risk Matrix: Prioritized list of findings based on severity and business impact.

Retest Report: Validation testing after remediation efforts are completed.

Test Your Defenses

Don't wait for attackers to find your vulnerabilities. Let our ethical hackers identify and help you fix security weaknesses before they're exploited.

Schedule a Pentest

Why this page should not be trusted

This is a harmless offline awareness demo for a school presentation. It is built to help students spot phishing signs without collecting any information.

1

Suspicious web address

The domain is not actually google.com. Attackers often hide the real domain in a long address.

2

“Not secure” warning

A sign-in page asking for a password should never look untrusted or insecure.

3

Urgent scare tactics

Messages like “disabled today” and “30 minutes” try to make people panic instead of think.

4

Unusual sender

The fake email sender is not a normal school or Google address.

5

Unexpected password request

If you got here from a link in an email or text, entering your password could hand it to an attacker.

If this were a real phishing page, typing a password here could give an attacker access to school email, cloud files, saved passwords, and any other account that reused the same password.
Correct response: do not sign in from the link. Instead, open a new browser tab and go directly to the real website, or contact your school using a known trusted method.

raspberry-pi-scanner.title: Raspberry Pi QR Scanner | Derek Nolt
raspberry-pi-scanner.description: Inside a Raspberry Pi check-in kiosk: camera processing, QR decoding, SQLite durability, asynchronous API delivery, and measured performance.
raspberry-pi-scanner.body:
DN Derek Nolt
  • About
  • Experience
  • Projects
  • Skills
  • Contact
← All projects

Hardware & Automation

Raspberry Pi QR Scanner

Inside a Raspberry Pi check-in kiosk: camera processing, QR decoding, SQLite durability, asynchronous API delivery, and measured performance.

By Derek Nolt

A kiosk with a simple job and several moving parts

The scanner is a headless check-in kiosk for the Ohio Furniture Market. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W and Camera Module 3 Wide read attendee QR badges, while Python handles decoding, local persistence, and delivery to the check-in API. Three traffic-light LEDs, a 60-pixel WS281x strip, and a passive buzzer provide the operating interface.

The interesting engineering problem is keeping those parts independent. A badge can be in view while a previous API request is still running. A buzzer can be sounding while another frame arrives. A network outage should not turn a locally recorded scan into an invisible failure.

Keep frames fresh instead of building a backlog

Picamera2 captures YUV420 frames. The capture worker copies the luminance plane needed for QR decoding and releases the camera request before the decoder starts work. A one-slot buffer keeps the latest frame: if the decoder falls behind, a newer image replaces the waiting image rather than joining a growing queue.

The decoder searches a center crop first. If that misses, it immediately tries the full frame; it also searches the full frame every third processed frame even after a crop succeeds. That periodic wider search helps find badges outside the center. The source supports both pyzbar and an optional ZXing backend, restricted to QR codes.

Camera → latest luminance frame → QR decoder
                                  ↓
                         bounded persistence queue
                                  ↓
                            SQLite commit
                             ↙          ↘
                    local feedback    API workers
                                          ↓
                                confirmation or retry

Source defaults and the installed configuration

The source defaults request 640 × 480 capture at 30 FPS, a 384 × 384 center crop, pyzbar decoding, and manual focus. The installed kiosk profile documented on October 7, 2026 uses 1280 × 960 capture, a 768-pixel crop, ZXing, and continuous autofocus with full range and fast speed. Requested camera FPS is a configuration value, not a measurement of completed scans per second.

SCANNER_WIDTH=1280
SCANNER_HEIGHT=960
SCANNER_CROP_SIZE=768
SCANNER_DECODER=zxingcpp
SCANNER_FOCUS_MODE=continuous
SCANNER_AF_RANGE=full
SCANNER_AF_SPEED=fast

Camera settings live in configuration rather than being scattered through the application. Capture, decoding, persistence, feedback, and metrics also have separate modules, which makes it easier to tune one part without changing the API contract.

A recorded scan is different from a confirmed check-in

A valid badge enters a bounded persistence queue with 20 slots. The persistence worker commits it to a SQLite outbox before producing the local SAVED feedback: a brief green strip flash and two beeps. That feedback means the scan is recorded locally. Server confirmation happens afterward.

If the persistence queue is full, the scanner reports a busy condition rather than pretending to accept the badge. This is a deliberate boundary: a frame that was decoded but never committed is not a durable scan. Items still waiting in memory can be lost during abrupt power loss.

The QR parser extracts the first company_id and attendee query values. The application sends those with a scanner_id in a JSON POST to a configured endpoint, using an X-Scanner-Token header. Two API workers normally run with reusable HTTP sessions. The scanned URL itself is not fetched; its host and path are not currently validated by the payload parser.

Recovery, retries, and duplicate delivery

Retryable outcomes stay in the outbox, with exponential retry delays starting at five seconds and capped at five minutes. On restart, pending records are available for replay. Definitive responses remove the corresponding outbox entry. A unique payload constraint prevents multiple pending copies of the same badge.

Delivery is at least once. If the API accepts a check-in and the kiosk loses power before recording that outcome, the same record can be sent again. The server therefore needs idempotent check-in handling. Local deduplication reduces repeats, but cannot replace that server-side rule.

A separate in-memory history is bounded to 10,000 payloads and 24 hours; it resets when the program restarts. Operational logs use a shortened SHA-256 fingerprint instead of printing the complete badge payload. The SQLite outbox still contains badge data: owner-only file permissions restrict access but do not encrypt it.

What the documented measurements actually show

The project notes record five repeated decodes of one saved 1280 × 960 badge frame. ZXing had a median decode time of 16.6 ms, compared with 154.5 ms for pyzbar using the scaled center crop, and both returned the same payload. This compares decoders on that image; it is not a general throughput or reliability benchmark.

A separate five-presentation walk-up test successfully read all five presentations, with a mean GO-cue-to-first-read time of 1.146 seconds. Those timings include the person’s reaction and badge movement. They do not isolate autofocus time. A stationary lighting comparison read 226/226 frames with white illumination and 228/228 with the strip off, with medians around 14 ms; that does not establish performance for moving badges or other rooms.

These are previously documented project measurements, not new benchmarks run for this article. The distinction matters: decoding a saved image, acquiring a moving badge, and waiting for a server reply measure different parts of the experience.

Testing the failure paths

Hardware-independent tests cover the commit-before-feedback boundary, a blocked API while new scans continue saving, queue backpressure, retry recovery, and shutdown behavior. Metrics separate capture, decoding, persistence, API, and feedback latency rather than combining them into one number.

The application can run under systemd for restart after failure or reboot. The main lesson from the design is to make each state observable: seeing a QR code, saving a scan, and confirming a check-in are separate events, and the software and physical feedback should preserve that distinction.

Security Assessment

What is a Security Assessment?

A security assessment is a comprehensive evaluation of your organization's information security posture. Our expert team conducts thorough analysis of your systems, processes, and policies to identify vulnerabilities, assess risks, and provide actionable recommendations to strengthen your security defenses.

Unlike penetration testing which focuses on exploiting vulnerabilities, a security assessment takes a holistic approach to evaluate your entire security ecosystem, including technical controls, administrative policies, and physical security measures.

Security Research

Threat Detection & Research

How I connect security research, endpoint and email evidence, lab validation, and practical incident response.

By Derek Nolt

Start with a question the evidence can answer

My security work includes configuring Wazuh and Microsoft 365 Defender, maintaining IT infrastructure, and helping restore operations after a ransomware incident. The research side of that work is about understanding how activity becomes visible: what a system records, what an alert means, and what remains unknown.

A useful investigation needs a specific question. An unexpected process, a suspicious email, and a new network connection may be related, but their proximity alone does not establish a chain of events. The goal is to build an explanation that can be checked against the available records.

Build a timeline before drawing a conclusion

For endpoint activity, useful fields to look for include the device, account, timestamp, process name, parent process, command line, and any associated destination or file hash. Availability depends on the telemetry and configuration. For email, the analogous context includes the recipient, message identifiers, delivery information, and the URLs or attachments involved.

A practical timeline keeps the raw event time and its time zone alongside a normalized time. It also records the source of each observation. That makes it possible to revisit an apparent sequence without confusing when something happened with when an alert was generated or reviewed.

Time (UTC) | Source | Device / account | Observation | Evidence reference
[time]     | [log]  | [entity]         | [fact]      | [event or capture ID]

Use lab work to test an explanation

Hack The Box Academy and home lab work support my study of Active Directory, network environments, and bug bounty methodology. A lab is useful for asking a narrow question and repeating the same action while observing its traces. It also makes it easier to identify missing telemetry before relying on it during an incident.

A repeatable exercise records the starting configuration, the action, the expected evidence, and the observed result. If an expected event is absent, check collection and parsing before treating that absence as proof that the action did not happen. A test result should describe the environment it actually covers.

From an alert to a detection hypothesis

Consider a hypothetical alert involving a command interpreter. The process name alone provides little context: administrators and business software use those tools too. Parent process, command line, account, and nearby activity can help distinguish an ordinary task from something that needs investigation. This is an example of the reasoning process, not a claim about a specific incident.

The next step is to state a detection hypothesis and test both suspicious and ordinary examples. Document why a condition was selected, which legitimate workflows might match it, and what evidence would justify escalation. An exception should be narrow enough that its purpose remains understandable when someone revisits it later.

Connect investigation to recovery

Helping with ransomware recovery tied security monitoring directly to operations for me. Identifying the compromise path, removing the attack vector, and restoring service require both technical evidence and an understanding of how the environment is used.

That experience shapes the questions I want research to answer: which records would help reconstruct the event, which controls would interrupt the path, and how would we verify the environment after remediation? The useful output is a finding or improvement that another person can understand, reproduce, and act on.

Embedded Security

UART & IoT Pentesting

A technical walkthrough of UART testing: electrical identification, boot captures, console access, and evidence-based IoT findings.

By Derek Nolt

The question behind the connector

A device can have a polished web interface and still expose a very different view of its internals on a circuit board. That is what interests me about UART testing: following the connection between physical hardware, startup behavior, and the software controls that protect a system. This article lays out a testing workflow; it does not claim a confirmed vulnerability in a particular product.

A useful investigation starts with a concrete question. Does the interface only print diagnostics? Does it accept input? Does it expose a login prompt or an interactive console? Those are different outcomes, and the evidence should make the distinction clear.

Identify the electrical interface first

UART sends asynchronous serial data over transmit and receive lines. A connection needs a shared ground, with the device’s TX connected to the adapter’s RX and, when interaction is needed, the device’s RX connected to the adapter’s TX. The adapter’s logic level must match the target. Logic-level UART and RS-232 are not electrically interchangeable. SparkFun’s wiring guide explains the signal-level distinction.

Before connecting an adapter, document the board revision and candidate pads, check the component documentation, and measure the interface. A connector’s shape does not establish its pinout or voltage. Begin by observing the target’s transmit line; add a transmit connection only after the interface is understood. Keep the target’s power arrangement explicit rather than assuming the adapter should power the board.

Capture a complete boot sequence

A readable capture depends on matching baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits. For example, Espressif documents 115200 baud with eight data bits, no parity, and one stop bit for the ESP32 console. That is a documented example, not a universal IoT setting. Resetting the board with a terminal already open captures the early output that would otherwise be missed. Espressif’s serial connection guide also covers port identification and terminal setup.

Keep the raw capture and an accompanying note with the board revision, firmware version if known, adapter, voltage, serial settings, and reset method. Mark where the output changes from early boot to the application. A later reader should be able to tell whether a message appeared on every boot or only after an interaction.

Separate bootloader access from application access

A bootloader prompt, an operating-system login, and an application command interface have different capabilities. On a U-Boot-based device, commands such as coninfo describe console devices, while env print displays environment variables when those commands are included in the build. These can help explain the boot configuration without changing it. Command availability depends on the firmware. See the console information and environment command documentation.

The presence of a prompt does not establish unrestricted access. Record which operations are available and which are denied, then connect that observation to the security question. Keep configuration changes separate from initial observation so the evidence still describes the device’s original behavior.

Turn console output into testable findings

OWASP’s UART test cases cover console authentication, bootloader access, sensitive information in serial output, and command input handling. They provide a useful structure for checking both the startup path and normal operation. A finding should identify what access is required and the capability actually demonstrated. Production controls may include restricting console access and removing unnecessary diagnostic disclosure. OWASP UART testing guide.

For a report, pair each claim with a short, reproducible observation. “Boot output contains a software version” is different from “the console accepts commands without authentication.” Record the conditions, the expected behavior, the observed behavior, and the reason the difference matters. Redact credentials or identifying data in any excerpt intended for publication.

What a useful lab record looks like

Device / board revision: [record exact markings]
Firmware: [version and how it was identified]
Interface: [pad locations, measured logic level]
Connection: [adapter and serial settings]
Capture: [cold boot / reset / normal operation]
Access observed: [output only / login / console]
Evidence: [capture timestamps and repeatable steps]
Impact: [capability demonstrated, not assumed]

The part I find most interesting is moving from an electrical signal to an explanation of system behavior. Good notes make that process repeatable: another test can distinguish a firmware change, a wiring issue, and a real change in access. Device-specific captures and verified results would turn this workflow into a case study.
